A society is rarely a closed politico-juridical system. To
explain the genesis of the modern world, we must abandon
the sovereign state as the primary unit of analysis.
The modern world-economy is an entity larger than any
juridically defined political unit- a single social system
linked by economic flows rather than political boundaries.

Empires collapse under the weight of their own political superstructures
For 5,000 years, world-economies inevitably transformed into empires. Empires collect tribute, which equates to
payments received for protection- but often in excess of the cost of producing that protection. The genius of the
capitalist world-economy is its ability to increase the flow of surplus from the periphery to the center without the
wasteful overhead of a unified political state.

Agronomy dictated vastly different geographic destinies for Europe and China
In the 15th century, China and Europe possessed roughly equal populations and similar technological baselines.
However, Europe's reliance on meat and wheat demanded five to six times more land to produce a single calorie of
food compared to vegetable crops. While Europe suffered a profound lack of space, condemning it to the conquest
of the Earth, China lacked men, driving its expansion inward.

'Systemic expansion required specific material and psychological commodities
European expansion was not driven by the luxury spice trade, but by an urgent demand for bulk staples:
food and fuel. Furthermore, Europe required precious metals not merely as commodities, but to build
collective psychological confidence. In an era of fragile credit mechanisms, bullion was the essential hedge
required to underwrite the massive risks of an emerging capitalist market.

State machineries upgraded their bureaucratic and
military extraction capabilities
To survive the transition, western European states had to transition from ad-hoc feudal levies to standing armies
equipped with expensive artillery. Monarchs utilized tax-farming and the sale of bureaucratic offices to bypass the
traditional nobility and secure independent financial resources. The state became less of a traditional sovereign
and more of a central economic enterprise, securing monopoly rights and favorable terms of trade.

Cartography of Capitalism
American bullion interacted with monetary velocity
to ignite a price revolution
The influx of precious metals did not just passively cause inflation; it provided the vital liquidity necessary to
sustain economic expansion. Bullion acted as a floor that prevented prices from collapsing during agrarian
downturns. The resulting drop in interest rates dramatically lowered the cost of capital, penalizing hoarded
wealth and heavily incentivizing speculative investment.

Capital accumulation relied on structural illusions and delayed payments
The catastrophic drop in real wages was heavily dependent on the remnants of precapitalist social
structures. Without modern trade unions, price indexes, or regular payment schedules, the working class
was structurally incapable of maneuvering against galloping inflation. Capitalism utilized these archaic
rigidities to systematically extract surplus value from the labor force.

A new global division of labor emerged to feed the core states
By 1640, the European world-economy was defined by a strict geographical division of labor. The
periphery was locked into providing low-cost raw materials via slavery and serfdom (e.g., Baltic grain
grain constituted 23% of Dutch consumption). This systemic inequality allowed the core states to
specialize in high-margin industries and capital accumulation.
